content.text: **One brain for you and your company, read by every agent you use.** Put your own notes and your company's docs in one place: a facts page, a decisions log, call transcripts. Claude Code, Codex and your other agents look there before they answer, so they stop starting from zero and work from what you and your team actually wrote down. GBrain is MIT-licensed and free to self-host, and it starts with no API keys: search is by keyword until you add one. gbrain.io is optional paid hosting. > [!TIP] > **Need hosted? First time running an agent?** Try **[gbrain.io](https://gbrain.io/?ref=readme)**, hosted GBrain, for the easiest experience: one brain for you and your team, connected to ChatGPT, Claude and Cursor, with nothing to install or keep online. Stuck? Email support@gbrain.io and a person will set it up with you, free. **A few minutes after you install it:** - Every new Claude Code or Codex session looks in your brain before it answers, without being told to. - Anything you ask your agent to remember is still there in the next session, in every agent connected to the brain. - Your notes and your company's docs are searchable, and your agent answers questions like *"what did we decide about pricing, and why?"* from them. **Works with these agents** (each name links to its guide): | How it connects | Agents | |---|---| | One command wires memory, hooks and instructions | [Claude Code](docs/mcp/CLAUDE_CODE.md) (`gbrain setup claude-code`), [Codex](docs/mcp/CODEX.md) (`gbrain setup codex`) | | `gbrain setup hermes` registers MCP through Hermes's own CLI and adds the brain-first instructions | [Hermes](#hermes) | | MCP from its guide, then `gbrain setup ` adds the brain-first instructions | [OpenClaw](docs/mcp/OPENCLAW.md), [opencode](docs/mcp/OPENCODE.md), [Cursor](#connect-gbrain-to-your-ai-client-mcp) | | MCP from its guide | [ChatGPT](docs/mcp/CHATGPT.md), [Claude Desktop](docs/mcp/CLAUDE_DESKTOP.md), [Claude Cowork](docs/mcp/CLAUDE_COWORK.md), [Perplexity](docs/mcp/PERPLEXITY.md), [Grok Build](docs/mcp/GROK.md), [Grok Bot](docs/guides/grok-bot.md), [Muse](docs/guides/muse.md), [Windsurf and other stdio clients](#connect-gbrain-to-your-ai-client-mcp) | | Any other coding agent | Paste the [install prompt](#heres-how-to-self-host-it) below | ## Stability New releases come out many times a day, but the install command below gives you the **stable channel**: a release reaches it only after the full test suite and a two-hour, 600,000-page load test pass on that exact release, and only when an important fix is waiting or stable is a week old. Updates are never installed without your say-so unless you turn on automatic upgrades. After an upgrade, gbrain shows a one-time notice listing what changed in behaviour. Stable also comes with a written promise about which commands, flags, tools, config keys and output fields stay the same, and how much warning you get before one changes. [docs/STABILITY.md](docs/STABILITY.md) explains that promise, how often stable moves, how to pin a version or go back, and what the faster alpha channel is for. ## Install > [!TIP] > **Fastest: hosted GBrain at [gbrain.io](https://gbrain.io/cli?ref=readme), for any harness.** One command launches a GBrain hosted on gbrain.io; Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT, Cursor and every other AI you use connect to it, with nothing to keep online. > > ```bash > curl -sSL https://gbrainio.terminalwire.sh | bash > gbrainio terminal connect # in a new terminal > gbrainio workspace new # pick a plan in the browser > curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash # skip if Bun 1.4.4+ is installed > export PATH="$HOME/.bun/bin:$PATH" > bun install -g github:garrytan/gbrain#stable # the gbrain CLI only; no local brain > # Claude Code (an existing gbrain entry is kept): > (claude mcp get gbrain >/dev/null 2>&1 || claude mcp add --transport http --scope user gbrain https://gbrain.io/mcp) && gbrain setup claude-code --instructions-only > # Codex (an existing gbrain entry is kept): > (codex mcp get gbrain >/dev/null 2>&1 || codex mcp add gbrain --url https://gbrain.io/mcp) && gbrain setup codex --instructions-only > ``` > > Bun's installer needs `unzip` and stops with `error: unzip is required to install bun` without it. Check with `command -v unzip`; if it prints nothing, install it first: `apt-get update && apt-get install -y unzip` (Debian, Ubuntu), `dnf install -y unzip` (Fedora, RHEL) or `apk add unzip` (Alpine), with `sudo` in front unless you are root. No way to install packages? Use the [no-unzip route](INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md#no-unzip), not an improvised one. A command scanner (Hermes) refuses the Bun installer or `bun install -g`? Use the [release binary route](INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md#release-binary). > > `gbrain setup --instructions-only` tells the agent the brain is there; agents seldom call an MCP server nobody told them about. It writes the [brain-first block](docs/guides/setup.md#brain-first-instructions) into `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` or Codex's `AGENTS.md` (a non-empty `AGENTS.override.md` instead when Codex has one) with a per-turn rule hook, and leaves the MCP entry alone; the same command with `--no-instructions` added takes them out. > > The installer is a shell script for macOS and Linux; read it before you run it. ### Here's how to self-host it GBrain is MIT-licensed and free to self-host. It needs **Bun 1.4.4 or newer**; existing worker installs read the [authorization and queue upgrade guide](docs/guides/authorization-upgrade.md) before restarting on this version. > [!WARNING] > **GBrain is NOT distributed on npm.** The npm `gbrain` package is unrelated and > can shadow the real binary, so never run `npm install -g gbrain` or > `bun add -g gbrain`. Install only via `bun install -g github:garrytan/gbrain#stable` > (the soaked stable channel; `#latest-stable` is the alpha line with every release) > or `git clone --branch stable` + `bun install && bun link`. Installed by mistake? `gbrain doctor` gives the fix. > Schema not migrated ([#218](https://github.com/garrytan/gbrain/issues/218))? Run > `gbrain apply-migrations --yes --no-autopilot-install`; if it exits 1, run `gbrain doctor --json`, not another `--yes` (`wedged`: relay its fix). ```bash bun install -g github:garrytan/gbrain#stable gbrain setup claude-code # or: gbrain setup codex gbrain init --pglite --no-embedding # any other harness, or no agent ``` `gbrain setup` shows what it will write first (`--dry-run` previews, `--remove` undoes), creates a keyless brain only if none exists, wires MCP, hooks and a brain-first block in the agent's instruction file (`--no-instructions` skips it), and smoke-tests them ([setup guide](docs/guides/setup.md)). For any other coding agent, paste: ```text Add GBrain memory to this existing agent. Read and follow: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/garrytan/gbrain/master/INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md Keep my current identity and instructions, start keyless, and show me the search-mode choice. Verify a remember/recall round trip with real GBrain calls. ``` ### Hermes Hermes checks every shell command before it runs it, and with nobody there to approve (`hermes chat -q`, a gateway or cron run) it refuses the Bun installer and `bun install -g`. Install the release binary instead, one file that needs no Bun and no package install, and let setup register it through Hermes's own `hermes mcp add`. Run each line as its own command (Linux x64; on an Apple Silicon Mac use `gbrain-darwin-arm64`): ```bash curl -fL --create-dirs -o ~/.local/bin/gbrain https://github.com/garrytan/gbrain/releases/latest/download/gbrain-linux-x64 chmod +x ~/.local/bin/gbrain ~/.local/bin/gbrain init --pglite --no-embedding ~/.local/bin/gbrain setup hermes ``` Then start a new Hermes session. Setup registers the MCP server (`hermes mcp test gbrain` checks it) and adds the brain-first rule to `~/.hermes/SOUL.md` with a per-turn hook. Hermes's approval and command-scanner settings stay as they are; setup only records the approval for its own per-turn hook. If setup prints a `hermes mcp add` command instead of registering, run that command as printed. To paste it to Hermes instead, use the prompt above. Details: [docs/mcp/HERMES.md](docs/mcp/HERMES.md). Postgres, thin clients, API keys and upgrades: [docs/INSTALL.md](docs/INSTALL.md). Agents: [INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md](INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md). Memory-only walkthrough: [give your coding agent a memory](docs/tutorials/connect-coding-agent.md). ### Add your notes and your company's docs Point GBrain at two folders of Markdown files: your own notes (an Obsidian vault works) and your company's docs. In the company folder, keep `facts.md` (numbers and statements agents may repeat), `decisions.md` (each decision with its date, its reason and who made it) and call transcripts saved as `.md` files. ```bash gbrain sources add notes --path ~/notes --federated --force # your notes gbrain sources add company --path ~/company --federated --force # company docs gbrain sync --all # rerun after edits ``` Then open a new agent session and ask *"What did we decide about a free plan, and why?"*: the answer comes from your decisions log. `--federated` puts the folder in default search, and `--force` accepts a folder that isn't a git repository; in a folder that is one, GBrain reads only committed files, so commit your edits before you sync. To see the shape first, `gbrain sources demo company-brain` runs a fictional company in a few seconds without touching your brain. Before you share a company brain with a team, read the [company-brain tutorial](docs/tutorials/company-brain.md). GBrain is not a data warehouse or analytics store. Keep ads, analytics, CRM and payment data in your warehouse, and connect your agent to it separately. ### CLI standalone (no agent) ```bash gbrain init --pglite --no-embedding # keyless; no server, no Docker gbrain import ~/notes/ --no-embed # index your markdown gbrain search "a phrase from a note" --json gbrain doctor # verify health ``` ### Optional: a new personal agent To have GBrain create a **new persistent personal agent** with identity files and its own private GitHub repo, open Codex (CLI or ChatGPT desktop) or Claude Code in a new, empty folder and paste: ``` Read and follow every step of: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/garrytan/gbrain/stable/BOOTSTRAP_FOR_AGENTS.md Goal: set yourself up as my persistent personal agent in this folder, with gbrain as your memory. Interview me before writing any identity file — never invent answers. Ask before anything destructive. You are not done until `gbrain bootstrap verify` exits 0. ``` The repo is not a complete backup; see the [bootstrap guide](docs/guides/bootstrap.md). For the always-on version (24/7 ingestion and the overnight dream cycle on a server with 8GB+ RAM and its own API usage), run GBrain under [OpenClaw](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw) or [Hermes](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent) and point it at `INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md`; the [personal-brain tutorial](docs/tutorials/personal-brain.md) walks it end to end. ### Connect GBrain to your AI client (MCP) - **Local stdio client:** `gbrain setup claude-code` or `gbrain setup codex` registers `gbrain serve` (lists the memory verbs; `--surface full` lists every tool) behind gbrain's launcher, so a session opened in a cloned repository never loads that repository's `bunfig.toml` or `.env`, and adds the brain-first instructions: agents seldom call a brain nobody told them about. Cursor, Windsurf and other stdio clients take `"$(command -v gbrain)" serve --surface starter --advertise verbs`. - **Plugins with curated skills:** Codex `codex plugin marketplace add garrytan/gbrain@codex-plugin` + `codex plugin add gbrain@gbrain`; Claude Code `/plugin marketplace add garrytan/gbrain` + `/plugin install gbrain@gbrain`. - **This brain from anywhere:** `gbrain mcp expose` publishes it on your Tailscale tailnet as a user service (`--funnel` for cloud agents such as Grok Bot, Muse and ChatGPT). [Guide](docs/guides/remote-mcp.md). - **A brain on another host:** `gbrain connect https://your-host/mcp --token *** --install` (add `--agent codex` for Codex). Hosted brains use [native OAuth or a private handoff](docs/guides/hosted-harness-access.md); dashboard, clients and permissions live in [MCP administration](docs/mcp/ADMIN.md). Per-client guides: [Claude Code](docs/mcp/CLAUDE_CODE.md) · [Codex](docs/mcp/CODEX.md) · [ChatGPT](docs/mcp/CHATGPT.md) · [Claude Desktop](docs/mcp/CLAUDE_DESKTOP.md) · [Claude Cowork](docs/mcp/CLAUDE_COWORK.md) · [Perplexity](docs/mcp/PERPLEXITY.md) · [Hermes](docs/mcp/HERMES.md) · [OpenClaw](docs/mcp/OPENCLAW.md) · [opencode](docs/mcp/OPENCODE.md) · [Grok Build](docs/mcp/GROK.md) · [Grok Bot](docs/guides/grok-bot.md) · [Muse](docs/guides/muse.md) · [everything MCP](docs/mcp/README.md). **Keep skills beside knowledge.** New local brains include memory skills in their content root. Agents can join an authorized catalog; only approved editors can publish. Managed coding-agent installs add an owned native router; restart and real-use verification are separate steps. Staged migration preserves sharing choices and personal edits. See [shared brain skills](docs/guides/shared-brain-skills.md). ## Choose your setup 1. **Add GBrain to my existing agent — recommended.** Keep your agent's identity and save memory inside its environment. No new personal-agent identity or private repository is required. Start with the guide for **[Grok Bot](docs/guides/grok-bot.md)**, **[Muse](docs/guides/muse.md)**, or **[Codex / Claude Code](docs/tutorials/connect-coding-agent.md)**. [Other harnesses](#connect-gbrain-to-your-ai-client-mcp). 2. **Use the brain on my own computer from everywhere.** One command publishes it over MCP on your Tailscale tailnet and keeps it running: `gbrain mcp expose` (add `--funnel` for cloud agents such as Grok Bot, Muse and ChatGPT). Follow **[use your brain from anywhere over MCP](docs/guides/remote-mcp.md)**. **Say to your agent:** *"use my brain over mcp"* — *"put my brain on tailscale"*. 3. **Connect my existing hosted brain.** Follow **[hosted harness access](docs/guides/hosted-harness-access.md)** to choose native OAuth or a private machine connection. For dashboard login, clients, and permissions, use **[MCP administration](docs/mcp/ADMIN.md)** with the server's separate owner credential. Delegation is an explicit choice. Grok **Bot** and Grok **Build** are different products. Muse's personal agent and **Muse Code** are different products too. Muse already has native editable memory; GBrain adds an explicit, portable record with provenance and shared access. See each guide's dated evidence and remaining verification steps. I'm Garry Tan, President and CEO of Y Combinator. I built GBrain to run my own AI agents. It's the production brain behind my OpenClaw and Hermes deployments: **155,795 pages, 24,589 people, 5,340 companies**, 66 cron jobs running autonomously. My agent ingests meetings, emails, tweets, voice calls, and original ideas while I sleep. It enriches every person and company it encounters. It fixes its own citations and consolidates memory overnight. I wake up smarter than when I went to bed — and so will you. **It works as a company brain too.** Authenticated remote clients are constrained by source and operation grants plus visibility filters. Local files and shared database credentials are a different trust boundary: sources alone do not isolate those callers. The authorization tests exercise specific access paths, not a universal no-leak guarantee. Read the [sharing boundaries](docs/architecture/brains-and-sources.md#what-confines-remote-callers-and-what-does-not) and [company-brain tutorial](docs/tutorials/company-brain.md) before setting up shared access. Alongside keyword and semantic retrieval, GBrain offers two optional ways to use your stored knowledge: - **A synthesis layer that gives you the actual answer.** Synthesized, well-cited prose across people, companies, deals, and ideas. Not "here are 10 chunks that mention your query"; an actual answer with citations and an explicit note on what the brain doesn't know yet. The gap analysis is the part that changes how you use the brain. - **A typed knowledge graph.** Trusted local page writes extract supported references without LLM calls when auto-linking is enabled. Remote `put_page` edges arrive later, via sweeps, maintenance or `add_link`. Ask "who works at acme-example?": walks are breadth-first, milliseconds on dense clusters ([how](docs/architecture/RETRIEVAL.md#breadth-first-graph-walks)). On BrainBench relationship questions, relationship retrieval lifts production **R@5 from 0.6626 to 0.7241** ([benchmark](docs/architecture/RETRIEVAL.md#the-benchmark)); 0.9791 is the `graph-oracle-parse` upper bound, not a product score. The point of building a 150K-page brain is to use it as a strategic moat. To never lose context. To query what's in your own head without re-reading it. The brain layer is what makes the moat usable. The 24/7 dream cycle is what keeps it sharp. Both run on your hardware, your DB, your keys. It's easier to ship a daemon that runs 24/7 to ingest, enrich, and consolidate than it is to keep an agent in chat working hard. GBrain is that daemon, generalized. Install in 30 minutes. Your agent does the work. As my personal agent gets smarter, so does yours. > **Start keyless.** Your harness subscription and any separately configured model API usage are different costs. The optional personal-agent bootstrap takes about 15 minutes; always-on enrichment needs its own compute and API configuration. Durable preferences and facts can be shared across agents; transient task and harness configuration state stay local. Configured cloud embedding, reranking, extraction, and synthesis providers can receive text, and the harness model sees recalled memory even in keyless mode. Markdown export is not a full database backup. Read [memory boundaries](docs/guides/memory-boundaries.md). > **LLMs:** fetch [`llms.txt`](llms.txt) for the documentation map, or [`llms-full.txt`](llms-full.txt) for the same map with core docs inlined in one fetch. **Agents:** start with [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md) (or [`CLAUDE.md`](CLAUDE.md) if you're Claude Code). ## What this looks like Say you have a meeting with Alice tomorrow. You want to walk in remembering what she works on, when you last talked, and what's still open between you. Here's what you'd type, and what you'd get back. **You ask:** > "What do I need to know before my meeting with Alice tomorrow?" **Most personal-knowledge tools give you back a list of pages.** Something like: ``` 1. people/alice — Alice runs engineering at Acme... 2. meetings/2026-03-15-alice-q1 — Q1 product review with Alice... 3. meetings/2026-01-08-acme-kickoff — Kickoff meeting with Acme team... 4. customers/acme — Acme is a series-B fintech we work with... 5. notes/2026-04-22 — Quick chat with Alice about pricing... ``` Five pages you now have to open and read yourself to actually prepare. The tool found the right material, but it didn't do the work. **GBrain gives you back the answer, with sources:** ``` Alice runs engineering at Acme (a series-B fintech). You last spoke on April 22 in a quick pricing chat. Three things are still open from that conversation: 1. She owes you the security review for the new tier (deadline was May 1; no update since). 2. You committed to pricing for a 500-seat tier (you sent it April 25; no response yet). 3. She mentioned they're hiring a CISO; you said you'd intro someone from your network. Heads up: nothing's been added to the brain about Alice or Acme since April 22, six weeks ago. She may have replied through email or Slack DM, channels the brain doesn't see. Worth asking her to catch up before assuming any of this is still current. ``` curl: (23) Failure writing output to destination
